paragraphs:
(A Roman emperor, beloved of our holy Rabbi.)
Hyman writes: We have already discussed this at length in the entry on R' Yehuda HaNasi, and here we shall merely record the places where he is mentioned in the Talmud and midrashim: Berakhot 57b, Sanhedrin 91a and 91b, Avodah Zarah 6a and 6b, and in the Jerusalem Talmud Shevi'it ch. 6 halakha 1, and Megillah ch. 1, supplied label מי״א (Mishnah 11), where Hyman reports that he converted through Rabbi; and Bereshit Rabbah ch. 75 sec. 5, ch. 84 sec. 3, and אס"ד ch. 1 sec. 16 [compare the Antoninus-and-Rabbi episode in the named Esther Rabbah 1:16].

Hyman reports that in Yuchasin, in the entry “R' Antoninus”, he cites that he is mentioned in the Mekhilta, tractate 'Vayehi' / Beshalach, where it says there: “R' Antoninus said: [A parable] of a king who sits in judgment on the platform”; and in the Sefer HaDorot he reads “R' Antigonus”, and likewise he cites from the Mekhilta Beshalach ch. 1: “R' Antigonus says: there were three.” And the Maskil LeEitan cites that the reading of the Vilna Gaon is “R' Antoninus”. Hyman argues: All of them erred in this; the truth is as in the reading of the Yalkut there, that Rabbi tells a story about Antoninus, his beloved. And this indeed is the intent of the Vilna Gaon there: Rabbi says three — Antoninus added one more. The Gaon, author of Erekh Milin, already discussed this at length in the entry 'Antoninus'. And what the rabbi designated דאה"וו cites in his commentary Middot Sofrim p. 33, dismissing all his words offhandedly, is without justification and without any proofs, just as he dismissed his precious words on the matter of Antoninus, that he was not Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, as the Gaon designated שי״ר held, and invented from his own mind things that have no basis. I already discussed this at length in the entry on R' Yehuda HaNasi.
And Hyman relates that in Kohelet Rabbah ch. 10 sec. 5, Antoninus Ze'ira, grandson of Antoninus Rabba, is mentioned, who asked Rabbi who would die first, and Rabbi answered him: 'I.'

notes.text: Unexpanded abbreviations/names kept in Hebrew; no expansion invented. אס"ד is retained literally; דאה"וו and שי"ר likewise unresolved; 'Yuchasin', 'Maskil LeEitan', 'Sefer HaDorot', 'Erekh Milin' are rendered by conventional identification of the Hebrew titles without verification.

The sentence 'Rabbi says three — Antoninus added one more' follows the Hebrew literally; its relation to the Vilna Gaon's gloss is as Hyman states it. Mekhilta locator 'מס' דויהי בשלח' is kept as printed.

Whole source/all notes read. Hyman owns polemic against other scholars, emperor identification, alleged readings and MarcusAurelius denial; these are attributed views, not root historical adjudication. למלך שהוא דן is the start of a parable OF a king, not RabbiAntoninus personally speaking TO a king. משכיל לאיתן is the cited work; דאה״וו designates the scholar and is not automatically a book authored byhim. SourceMeg1 מי״א retained as Mishnah11 rather than silently calledhalakhah11. אס״ד/דאה״וו/שי״ר remain source abbreviations/unresolved; no guessed expansions or authority merge. Final Rabbi answers I, not Antoninus answering himself. All inherited questions, variants and citedworkforms preserved. References to printed/native readings in inherited notes are preserved historical claims; this root pass uses supplied digital text and named saved editions, not a fresh pixel or correction-history verification.

The whole Torat Emet Esther Rabbah 1:16 paragraph recounts Antoninus making a feast for Rabbi and their dialogue. This is a positive named comparison for the supplied אס״ד 1:16, not a correction of its letters or proof of the separate conversion report. The whole Torat Emet Kohelet Rabbah 10:5 paragraph calls Antoninus Ze’ira the grandson of Antoninus Rabba and has him ask our holy Rabbi who will die first; Rabbi answers ‘I’, as Hyman’s short account states. These literary accounts do not identify a Roman emperor or admit their genealogy as an authority fact. The separate Yuchasin, Sefer HaDorot, Maskil LeEitan, Vilna Gaon, Yalkut, Erekh Milin and Middot Sofrim readings and arguments were not freshly collated; they remain Hyman’s reports and polemic, including ‘all erred’, ‘without justification and without any proofs’, his denial of the Marcus Aurelius identification and his accusation of invention. Their abbreviated personal titles and the uncollated Yehuda HaNasi pointer use R'; Rabbi where fully written רבי is retained. The supplied מי״א, אס״ד, דאה״וו, שי״ר, כדאת הגרון and רבי אומר ג׳ — הוסיף אנטונינוס עוד אחד remain unresolved source wording or attributions, without automatic expansion, printed correction history or identity binding. Both p001 and p002 source holds and all earlier mixed notes remain intact.

Hyman I, p. 231, prints Megillah 1:11 with a halakhah marker, beside the different marker מי״א in the supplied Hebrew. The named Jerusalem Talmud Megillah 1:11 passage expressly presents both conversion and nonconversion traditions. Hyman gives the affirmative account. Shevi’it 6:1 concerns a grant made for sharecropping, and the feast in Esther Rabbah 1:16 is a separate episode. The consulted Avodah Zarah 10a–b contains Antoninus and Rabbi exchanges beside Hyman’s printed and supplied 6a–b locator. Its different Severus relationships are preserved as local readings. The compact Esther siglum in the printed notice appears to end in ר, and the supplied letters אס״ד remain visible.

In the consulted Mekhilta, Vayehi Beshalach 1:26, Rabbi tells how Antoninus carried a lantern for his sons after holding court. In the consulted Yalkut Shimoni, Torah remez 230, Rabbi says that Antoninus added a further member of a chariot crew. The two passages have different settings. Hyman reads the transmitted attributions as referring to Antoninus in Rabbi’s account, and his criticism and judgment concerning Marcus Aurelius retain their force as his argument. The printed notice has כדעת הגאון שי״ר where the supplied text reads כדאת הגרון שי״ר. The consulted Seder HaDorot entry lists Antigonus in the Mekhilta’s Beshalach introduction and first chapter without quoting the words about three. Yuchasin’s account of Rabbi includes a separate report of secret conversion. Hyman’s specific Yuchasin quotation and his Maskil LeEitan, Gra, Erekh Milin and Middot Sofrim p. 33 comparisons remain attributed. The consulted Mekhilta edition’s identification in an editorial footnote and Hyman’s position are distinct.
